MSTP/G for audio vs. current web standards

Apple M4 Max, macOS 26.6.2, 44.1 kHz; Chrome 156.0.8078.47; Firefox 160.0a1 (patched to implement more standards); Safari 26.6.2

Overview
Stalls Receiver playback CPU contention Subnormals Timestamp alignment
Safari Running Code

Architecture

The source can be any MediaStream, such as a microphone, a media element playing, a remote track, etc.. Here it is a generated test signal.

Web standards

AudioWorklet, sinkless AudioContext (sinkId: { type: "none" }), SharedArrayBuffer. This can run in Firefox and Chrome (but not Safari just yet, see the Safari section for a complete list of missing APIs).

Variant 1: audioworklet: the processing runs in an AudioWorkletProcessor, not associated with an audio device ({sinkID: "none"}).

Variant 2: worker: the processing runs in a dedicated worker: AudioWorkletProcessor moves the audio through a SharedArrayBuffer buffer (classical SPSC design, ubiquitous: Chrome's solution, Firefox's solution). This is useful when using APIs that are best used on a Web Worker. Note that DIP is going to ship very soon, so SharedArrayBuffer is fine again (finally after 8 years!)

Variant 3, the classic with a twist: the same sinkless AudioContext as variant 1, whose AudioWorkletProcessors move audio to a dedicated worker and back, with postMessage or a ring buffer. The processing can use any worker API. postMessage needs no SharedArrayBuffer, but Shared memory is back on the menu, and might be preferable.

MSTP/G

mstp: MediaStreamTrackProcessor and MediaStreamTrackGenerator, with the processing in a dedicated worker. Chrome only.

Scenario

Two browsers on the same machine (to easily reproduce) are in a WebRTC call (or at least, one sends and one receive, it doesn't have to be duplex). The sender monitors its input (sends it to an audio output device). It also processes it using a type of processing that is not real-time safe: running this in the AudioWorkletProcessor on the AudioContext that is used for monitoring would glitch. The processed audio is then sent it to the receiver, which plays it (or does something e.g. mixes it, saves it, whatever). The sender also records the processed audio locally, as apps sometimes do for safety (sometimes called "local record" in podcasting apps).

Any 80 ms of the test signal tells where in the signal it comes from (see signal.js).

At each measurement point, we cross-correlate the audio with the signal to find how old it is (matching.py). Audio that doesn't match is counted as unmatched.

Various measurements happen:

  • Stalls: end to end latency (source on one machine to the other machine playback), in the presence of repeated 500ms stalls
  • Receiver playback: delay building up at the receiver's end: this let us determine if there's delay building up at the sending side or receiving side, to absorb the stalls
  • CPU contention: same deal, but with heavy audio processing, and the machine hammered by external load (64 stress-ng processes).
  • Timestamp alignments: same setup, with a sibling video stream, checking if A/V sync is satisfactory in those scenario. This test case can run well in Safari (that shows excellent results).

The processing is either a plain memory copy or a massive WebAssembly SIMD FIR filter (fir.wat), that has been measured as being roughly as fast to compute on all three browsers. Stalls are just busy-wait where they are to happen (AudioWorkletProcessor.process, etc.).

Measurement points:

  1. Source generated.
  2. Processing output.
  3. Local recording.
  4. Playback, getOutputTimestamp().
  5. Jitter buffer, getStats().

Every AudioContext runs at the device’s sample rate (on this machine, 44.1kHz). Again, we're using a single machine to repro easily, that means loopback network and no network latency.

In the tests, the browsers are headless, the sources are synthetic (AudioWorkletProcessor), to not depend on external stimuli on a microphone or complexify the setup using virtual audio driver. That means audio device latencies are mostly irrelevant.

Stalls

stalls · 22 s calls · 100, 200 and 500 ms stalls at 5, 10 and 15 s · block copy · 3 trials per arm

The processing stalls three times by busy-waiting where the processing runs (MediaStreamTrackProcessor, AudioWorkletProcessor, etc.). This simulates a slow plugin / processing pass, garbage collection pauses, heavy GPU processing would. During this time the source keeps producing audio. Real-time processing has to keep every sample, and to keep the recording’s timeline intact. It needs to catch up once it resumes, so that latency returns to where it was.

Columns

  • Render quantum. Frames per AudioWorklet process() call in the processing context.
  • Recorded audio intact. Trials whose MediaRecorder file (point 3) contains every 10 ms of the expected processed signal, in order and at the right level, after Opus.
  • Recording timeline intact. Trials whose WebM packet timestamps are contiguous within 2.1 ms, and whose container duration is within 40 ms of the decoded audio. Samples can be intact while their timestamps are not; players and editors then place them at the wrong time.
  • Catch-up after 500 ms stall. Per trial: time from the end of the 500 ms stall until the backlog is back under its pre-stall p95 plus one source batch, and stays there for 500 ms. “never”: not within the call.
  • Backlog before stalls. Source audio generated (point 1) but not yet out of the processing (point 2), 95th percentile before the first stall: the path’s steady-state buffering.
  • Source → playback before stalls. Median time from generation (point 1) to the receiver’s output device (point 4), before the first stall. Includes WebRTC and the receiver’s jitter buffer.

Failures and likely causes

From Chrome 156.0.8078.47 source.

Chrome audioworklet, 128 and 512 frames: audio lost, no catch-up. Chrome renders a sinkless AudioContext into a NullAudioSink, clocked in 10 ms steps. The stall blocks that render callback. The track feeding the context waits in a FIFO sized for six reads, about 60 ms here, and audio arriving once it is full is dropped. When the callback returns, the clock skips to the next on-time interval instead of rendering the time it missed, so the context never runs faster than real time and the backlog never drains. The render quantum doesn’t change this.

Chrome worker: no catch-up, timeline broken. The ring reader waits for the worker inside the sinkless context’s render callback, which blocks it for the stall. No audio is lost: the 2 s SharedArrayBuffer rings hold it. The clock then skips the intervals it missed, so the backlog stays in the output ring for the rest of the call. The processed track is stamped with the current time at each render, so after each stall its timestamps jump ahead while the samples continue: 78, 103 and 293 ms in the first trial, for the 100, 200 and 500 ms stalls.

Every Chrome path, including mstp: timeline jitter. MediaStreamAudioDestinationNode stamps audio with base::TimeTicks::Now() at render time, with a TODO to use the playout time. MediaRecorder’s Opus encoder derives packet timestamps from those capture times, not from a sample count. Render callbacks aren’t evenly spaced, so packet timestamps jitter by ±3 ms throughout every Chrome recording, against a 2.1 ms limit. MSTG passes the source’s AudioData timestamps through as capture times, so mstp inherits the source track’s jitter. In one trial the first packet is also stamped about 640 ms ahead of the next ones; the muxer forces later packets up to it, so 11 packets share timestamp 0.

Safari

Needs a sinkless AudioContext for both web standards paths, and renderSizeHint for the 512-frame variant (See Safari).

Receiver playback

playout · 60 s calls · 500 ms stall at 5 s · block copy · 3 trials per arm

One 500 ms stall in a 60 s call. Its backlog manifests on the other end as extra delay. We follow that delay at the receiver's output for the rest of the call, and split it between the sender's processing and the receiver's jitter buffer, to see where the audio waits and whether it drains, with things like a jitter buffer's compression strategy.

Failures and likely causes

Chrome worker: delay kept at the sender. Its added delay is not in the jitter buffer. The backlog stays in the sender’s output ring for the rest of the call, because Chrome’s sinkless context doesn’t render the time it missed (Stalls).

Chrome audioworklet, 128 and 512 frames: audio lost. Less delay is added because the stall’s audio is dropped at the sender instead of delivered late (Stalls).

Every other path: delay kept at the receiver. The stall’s audio reaches the receiver as a burst, about 500 ms late, and its jitter buffer keeps it. libwebrtc’s NetEq, in both browsers, accelerates only when playout delay exceeds its target plus the largest packet arrival delay of the last 2 s, so it plays normally until the burst ages out of that window. After that, each accelerate removes one pitch period, and only when the cut passes a 0.9 correlation test. Fast accelerate is off by default. The delay drains slowly, at a rate that depends on the signal.

Safari

Needs a sinkless AudioContext (sinkId: "none") for both web standards paths.

The other bits needed for this tests are already implemented in WebKit: getOutputTimestamp() and the jitter buffer counters (see Safari).

CPU contention

contention · 40 s calls · 16384-tap FIR · 64 stress-ng workers from 10 to 30 s · 128-frame render quantum · 3 trials per arm

The processing runs a 16384-tap FIR filter (that's a lot of taps), an eighth to a third of real time on this machine (Macbook pro M4 Max), while 64 stress-ng workers hammer every core for 20 s. Processing that loses the CPU falls behind: backlog and latency grow, and audio can be lost. This simulates either a machine that isn't fast enough (on the older/cheaper side), or a machine that is doing something heavy at the same time.

Columns

  • Phase. Before the load, during it (from 1 s after it starts), and after it (from 2 s after it ends).
  • Recorded audio intact. As in Stalls.
  • Backlog p95. Source audio generated but not yet out of the processing, 95th percentile per phase.
  • DSP ms per audio s. Wall-clock time spent in the filter per second of audio. Above 1000 would be above our real-time budget. This is wall clock, so it ticks while a processing thread is preempted.
  • Source → playback p50. Median time from generation to the receiver’s output device, per phase.
  • Jitter buffer target. Median jitterBufferTargetDelay per phase: the delay the receiver aims for.
  • Concealed under load. Audio the receiver synthesized using its jitter buffer during the load because packets arrived too late (concealedSamples).

Failures and likely causes

Firefox audioworklet control*: 37 ms lost in one trial. With real-time promotion disabled, the sinkless graph is starved during the load. Firefox’s cross-graph drift correction then underruns and, when input catches up, discards input above its desired buffering: a 37 ms skip 6.9 s into the load. The real-time configuration shows no such event.

Firefox worker: preempted under load. All audio is recorded, but backlog, latency and concealment grow during the load, and the filter takes longer per block. Thread priority doesn’t explain it: on macOS 26 both browsers run the worker at QOS_CLASS_USER_INITIATED (Firefox, Chrome). The cause is not identified yet.

Safari

Needs AudioContextOptions {sinkId: "none"}. As the control shows, rendering it on a real-time thread matters under load.

Subnormals

Floating-point numbers very close to zero (subnormals, or denormals) are slow on most x86 CPUs. Audio DSP produces them all the time: any filter, envelope or reverb tail decaying towards silence ends up there. Native audio code avoids the cost by having the CPU flush subnormals to zero. On the Web, this historically happened on the AudioWorkletProcessor.process. More recently, some engines removed this, which is unfortunately a breaking change. Mitigations can be put in place, but they aren't satisfactory, and are very invasive.

Firefox, like others, had to do this, but kept flushing to zero WebAssembly running in AudioWorkletProcessor.process(), and only there, as it always has. Code running anywhere else worker, where MSTP/G processing runs, doesn't get it.

The benchmark is simple, a cascade of four one-pole lowpass filters (y += a * (x - y)) whose impulse response decays into the subnormal range: the most common DSP code there is, found countless times in any non-trivial bit of audio code. It runs in JavaScript and in WebAssembly, without flushing. Each timing sample is a chunk of 65536 samples, 1.365 s of audio at 48 kHz; times are medians of 109 chunks before the filter state becomes subnormal and 71 after. Code: denormals/ (node bench.js, or open denormals.html).

Every Intel CPU tested is slow, including a 2025 high-end part, on both P-cores and E-cores. AMD Zen 3 has a small penalty: 2.9× in Wasm and 1.1× in JS, 1.18 ms against 7.65–57 ms on Intel. Apple silicon has none.

  • Slowdowns can't be compared across CPUs. A slowdown is the subnormal time divided by the normal time, so faster code shows a larger one on the same chip (73× for Wasm, 44× for JS on the J4125). Compare the subnormal times instead.
  • Times aren't clock-normalized. Tiger Lake against Panther Lake shows no improvement, but can't measure a small regression.

Without flushing

DSP in a worker, including MSTP/G processing, has no way to turn flushing on: WebAssembly and JavaScript can’t change the CPU’s floating-point mode. The code itself has to keep its state out of the subnormal range, in every site:

  • A noise floor in every recursive stage. In this benchmark, a 1e-18 DC offset on the input removes the penalty on every CPU tested. Real processing needs it at each filter, feedback loop, envelope and reverb, not once at the input: a DC blocker, a highpass filter or a gain downstream removes or scales the offset, and the states after it decay again. Tiny noise or an offset of alternating sign survives DC blockers.
  • Explicit flushing. Compare each state variable to a threshold and set it to zero, after every update. Faust’s -ftz option generates this. It costs a comparison per state per sample, and gets in the way of SIMD.

Native DSP code does neither. It relies on its host setting flush-to-zero on the audio thread (JUCE’s ScopedNoDenormals, for example), so compiled to WebAssembly it works as written in an AudioWorkletProcessor, where Firefox flushes. In a worker, the same off-the-shelf WebAssembly breaks: it is 38–73× slower on Intel as soon as a signal decays to silence, until each library is patched.

Conclusions

  • 76% of Firefox users are on affected hardware. Intel’s current high-end mobile part is 50× slower on subnormals. This won’t age out: newer or more expensive hardware doesn’t fix it.
  • The core type doesn’t matter. Panther Lake’s cpu0 and cpu15 are within 10% (8.97 and 9.89 ms), so pinning DSP threads to particular cores doesn’t help.
  • Where the processing runs matters. DSP in an AudioWorkletProcessor gets subnormals flushed to zero. The same DSP in a worker, as with MSTP/G, pays the full penalty on most users’ machines, unless every recursive stage of it is modified to avoid subnormals.

Timestamp alignment

timestamps · 22 s recordings · 100, 200 and 500 ms stalls at 5, 10 and 15 s · video clock +200, 0 and −200 ppm

A worker records audio while an independently clocked video source plays, as a recorder or a video call would. Each sample is multiplied by the gain of the video frame shown at its presentation time. The video clock runs 200 ppm fast, exactly on time, or 200 ppm slow, and the processing stalls three times. Audio and video stay aligned if every audio frame lands under the right video frame and the offset between them stays constant.

Columns

  • Video clock. The video source’s clock rate relative to the page.
  • Audio exact. The recording equals the source times the gain of the true frame at each sample’s presentation time, to float precision. Two negative controls confirm the check catches timing by processing time, and no gating.
  • Median offset. At each frame change in the recording: the source sample’s generation time minus the frame’s true start, median over the call. A constant offset can be calibrated; deviations from it can’t.
  • p95 deviation. 95th percentile of the distance from the median offset.
  • Max deviation around stalls. Largest distance from the offset measured outside stalls, from each stall’s start to 1 s after its end.

Failures and likely causes

None: every arm records the audio exactly and stays within about 4 ms of its offset.

Different median offsets. Not a failure: each engine puts presentation at a different point. The patched Firefox’s getOutputTimestamp() places a frame when it reaches the output device, after the output latency reported by the audio backend. That latency is read once per stream and includes a sampled timing gap, so Firefox’s offset varies between runs. WebKit stamps frames at render time, and Chrome’s mstp path uses AudioData timestamps taken at render time (Stalls), so both sit near zero.

Safari

Runs today. WebKit starts an AudioContext only with transient user activation, so the harness clicks the page before recording, and this is fine. On this test, Safari has the best performance of the three, as shown by the tightest deviation.

Running

Requirements:

  • uv for python
  • Chrome
  • An ffmpeg binary
  • A stress-ng binary for contention
  • A patched Firefox, and soon a Nightly/Release Firefox, patches are being reviewed. Optimized builds: Linux, Windows, macOS, Apple silicon, macOS, Intel, until 2026-11-20.
  • Safari for timestamps only

For Safari, running sudo safaridriver --enable and Develop -> Allow Remote Automation in the Preferences are necessary to enable remote control and remove human errors from the equation.

This framework uses browser automation to be able to reliably reproduces results.

Comments after the command show rough durations to run all tests a few times and regenerated the data (e.g. after patching or another machine). Running in parallel probably degrades the data quality in some cases, and we've preferred running everything linearly.

uv run repro trial --browser chrome --path mstp --out results/first   # One call, analyzed.
uv run repro --firefox /path/to/firefox run stalls                     # 18 min
uv run repro --firefox /path/to/firefox run playout                    # 65 min
uv run repro --firefox /path/to/firefox run contention                 # 30 min
uv run repro --firefox /path/to/firefox run timestamps --browsers chrome,firefox,safari
uv run --group dev pytest                                              # Analysis tests.
uv run python tools/build_site.py                                      # This page.

Output: results/<experiment>-<time>/. uv run repro summarize <directory> re-analyzes.
